S2.narr: Heat Shift Planner turns that into tomorrow's plan for site supervisors in Abu Dhabi.

S3.old: A fixed threshold tuned on eight US regions would put every Abu Dhabi day, June to September, in its top tier.

S4.narr: Abu Dhabi has no public data on work heat illness. So I used 2,628 US workplace heat hospitalisation reports. Frozen, then scored once on 86 case days in six regions it had never seen: it caught 79 percent, alerting on 49 percent of days.
S4.old: Abu Dhabi has no public data on work heat illness. So I tested on 2,628 heat hospitalisation reports from US federal OSHA. Frozen, then scored once in six US regions it had never seen: it caught 79 percent of reported-case days, alerting on 49 percent of days.

S5.narr: On the evening-before forecast: the same decision as the real weather on 84 percent of days.

S6.narr: I also trained a model. It ranked days better, but it learned hot places, not unusual days: in Abu Dhabi it would alert on almost every summer day. So the app keeps the rule.
S6.old: I pre-registered a test I expected to pass: incident reports as a trigger. On earlier fixed-threshold rules, it caught 11.6 points fewer heat days than a weather-only rule. So reports only prompt a check.

S7.narr: Whatever the forecast, the app shows the law: the midday break, and the heat stress programme from 35 degrees.
S7.old: Whatever the forecast, the law shows: the midday break, and the heat stress programme from 35 degrees. The Thermal Work Limit is not calculated.

S8.narr: Heavy work planned? Move heavy tasks away from the 2 p.m. peak. New or returning workers? 20 percent of usual heat exposure on day one, adding 20 percent a day.

S9.narr: On the seventh of July, the forecast adds no steps. A yes to new workers raises the tier one level, labelled as our rule.
